==English==

===Etymology===
From {{der|en|frm|adopter}}, from {{der|en|la|adoptō}}; {{compound|la|ad|optō|nocat=1|t2=to choose, desire}}, equivalent to {{af|en|ad-|opt}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/əˈdɒpt/|a=RP}}
* {{IPA|en|/əˈdɑpt/|a=GA}}
* {{audio|en|En-us-adopt.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɑpt|ɒpt|s=2}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}} {{tlb|en|transitive}}

# {{senseid|en|child}} To [[take]] (a child, heir, friend, citizen, etc.) by choice into a [[relationship]].
## To take voluntarily (a child of other parents) to be in the place of, or as, one's own child.
##: {{ux|en|A friend of mine recently '''adopted''' a Chinese baby girl found on the streets of Beijing.}}
## To obtain (a pet) from a shelter or the wild.
##: {{ux|en|We're going to '''adopt''' a Dalmatian.''}}
## To [[contribute]] towards the [[upkeep]] of (a child or animal), in exchange for occasional stories, pictures, etc.
##: {{ux|en|We '''adopted''' an elephant at the local zoo.}}
## {{senseid|en|responsibility}} To take by choice into the scope of one's responsibility.
##: {{ux|en|This supermarket chain '''adopts''' several families every Yuletide, providing them with money and groceries for the holidays.}}
# To take or receive as one's own what is not so naturally.
#: {{ux|en|He '''adopted''' a new look in order to fit in with his new workmates.}}
#* {{RQ:en:New York Times|author=w:Blake Bailey|title='Tennessee Williams,' by John Lahr [print version: Theatrical victory of art over life, ''International New York Times'', 18 November 2014, p. 13]|url=http://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/16/books/review/tennessee-williams-by-john-lahr.html|date=14 November 2014|passage=[S]he [Edwina, mother of {{w|Tennessee Williams}}] was indeed Amanda [Wingfield, character in Williams' play ''{{w|The Glass Menagerie}}''] in the flesh: a doughty chatterbox from Ohio who '''adopted''' the manner of a Southern belle and eschewed both drink and sex to the greatest extent possible.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250812205801/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/16/books/review/tennessee-williams-by-john-lahr.html|archivedate=12 August 2025}}
# To select and take or approve.
#: {{syn|en|espouse|embrace}}
#: {{co|en|to '''adopt''' the view or policy of another}}
#: {{ux|en|These are resolutions that were '''adopted'''.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1876|author=w:Henry Martyn Robert|title=w:Robert’s Rules of Order|location=Chicago|publisher=S.C. Griggs & Co.|section=Article XIV, Section 71, p. 156|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/9097/pg9097-images.html
|passage=Every society should '''adopt''' an order of business adapted to its special wants.}}
# {{lb|en|chess|slang}} To [[beat]] an [[opponent]] ten times in a row.
#: {{ux|en|The match was not even close; the IM made amateurish blunders and ended up getting '''adopted'''.}}
#* {{RQ:New Yorker|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220826233023/https://www.newyorker.com/culture/rabbit-holes/the-most-popular-chess-streamer-on-twitch|passage="That's it, that's it!" the Grandmaster Eric Hansen bellowed after following nine straight losses with a win. "You are not '''adopting''' me! Not today, not today!"|title=The Most Popular Chess Streamer on Twitch|date=2022-04-12|author=Jacob Sweet}}

====Usage notes====
In the sense of taking a child into one's family, Modern English makes a distinction between {{m|en|foster|fostering}} (which is implied to be temporary) and {{m-self|en|adopt|adopting}} (which is permanent and makes the child legally recognized as part of the family). In older usage, the two terms were more interchangeable.
